findings.element: states.day in render-b.js: .b-dayNote, the .b-dayNow section, behindBlock read at the wedding-day clock, and foot()
findings.problem: The morning of the wedding is the one screen the whole company is judged on, and it is the worst-written screen in the set. Driving state=day, the words under the couple's names read, in order: "This is the day the plan was for." (past tense, and it is about the plan rather than about the day), then "Happening now / Wedding day" (a database state label over a title that repeats "Wedding day at The Orchard" from 200px above, so the phrase is printed twice on one phone screen), then "Behind you / Venue walk-through, 19 September. The city hotel shortlist is not going ahead." The last full sentence a couple and their guests read on the morning is an admin task and a cancelled hotel search. Under that sits a footer stamped "Updated 15 July 2026", eleven weeks stale, which on the day itself reads as neglect. Every one of these strings is correct and none of them is right. The fold rule that serves a guest in July, naming the last thing done and the thing not going ahead, is the wrong rule on the one clock where the past is a keepsake rather than a status.
findings.fix: In states.day: (1) delete the .b-dayNote paragraph, because "Today", the names, "Saturday 3 October 2026" and "Wedding day at The Orchard" already say everything and the sentence only weakens them. (2) Suppress the .b-dayNow section when the only live item is the anchor itself (todayItems[0].date === F.project.primaryDate.date), since the header has already said it; keep the section only when a non-anchor item is dated that day. (3) Give behindBlock a day-of branch: when clock === F.project.primaryDate.date, set note = done.length + " things got you here, from " + F.fmt.medium(done[0].date) + " to " + F.fmt.medium(last.date) + "." and drop the cancellation clause entirely, because a plan dropped in April is not news on 3 October; on that branch change the .b-behindLabel from "Behind you" to "How you got here". (4) Give foot() an optional stamp argument and pass none on the day state, so the morning footer reads "Kept by Orla" and "Signal Timeline" only. Add a gate assertion that state=day contains neither "Updated" nor "not going ahead".

findings.element: bar() action act("Add a moment", ...) and the name === "add" branch of wireOwner in render-b.js
findings.problem: The owner's primary bar carries three buttons and one of them lies. Pressing "Add a moment" opens the editor on the first existing item: the title field comes up pre-filled with "Menu tasting at The Orchard" and the row count stays at seven. An owner who presses it and starts typing is silently renaming an existing moment. This is the defect class the library calls the worst there is, a labelled control performing an unrelated and unannounced action, and it is also a direct breach of this direction's own stated rule that anything not built has no button element. The behaviour gate cannot see it: the dead-control check only asserts that every button carries a data-act, and "add" carries one.
findings.fix: Build it. In the "add" branch create a new row rather than reusing one: build a .b-item with data-id = "new-" + Date.now(), data-away set to the first whole day after the nearest existing item, data-visibility "shown" and an empty .b-title, append it to .b-measure, call place(), then openEditor on it and focus #b-edit-title with an empty value and the placeholder "What is happening". Until the moment carries a title its row reads "Untitled moment", and the reversibility bar records "A new moment was added." If it is not being built this round, replace act("Add a moment", ...) with inert("Add a moment") so it stops advertising a verb, exactly as owner-empty already does with "Nothing to preview yet". Add a gate assertion: pressing "Add a moment" raises the .b-item count by one and leaves #b-edit-title empty and focused.

findings.element: paintUndo() and the .b-ceiling note in render-b.js
findings.problem: The editor speaks in exactly two places and gets both wrong. First, the reversibility bar is headed "Last change:" and it is not the last change. Press "Move a week earlier" and it reads "Last change: Send the invitations moved 7 days closer." The button says earlier, the receipt says closer, so one gesture has two names, and "closer" is not the antonym of "later", which is what the bar prints in the other direction. Switch the same item to Hidden and the bar still reports the date move: the most consequential thing an owner can do to what a guest sees leaves no record and cannot be undone. Delete a moment and the bar goes blank, so the one irreversible action also erases the record of the change before it while still calling itself the last change. Second, press +7 at the ceiling and the note that appears reads "The day itself is in 79 days." one line under a readout that already says "Saturday 3 October 2026 · in 79 days". It restates a number the reader is looking at and never says that the press was refused, or why.
findings.fix: In paintUndo, drop the "Last change: " prefix (the bar is a status region and the sentence stands alone) and change the direction pair from "closer."/"later." to "earlier."/"later." so the receipt uses the same words as the buttons that cause it; update the gate regex from /Send the invitations moved 7 days closer/ to /Send the invitations moved 7 days earlier/. Push a history entry from setVisibility reading "Send the invitations is now hidden from guests." (and "... is now shown to guests.") and from the delete branch reading "Send the invitations was removed.", each with an undo that restores the previous state rather than clearing the stack. Replace the .b-ceiling string with "Nothing can be moved past the wedding day." and update the gate assertion from /day itself/ to /past the wedding day/.

findings.element: field(), foot() and the refusal hint in states["owner-empty"] of render-b.js
findings.problem: The brand-new project belongs to Aisling & Tom: the bar says so and the h1 says so. Two facts on the same screen belong to Mara & Finn. field() hard-codes F.project.name, so the region a screen reader announces on this screen is "The plan for Mara & Finn". foot() hard-codes F.updatedLabel, so a project that has never held anything is stamped "Updated 15 July 2026", a date lifted from another couple's file and printed as a fact about this one. This is the fixture-leak class from the defect library creeping back in a new form: not an invented name this time, a real name attached to the wrong screen. On the same screen the refusal reads "Pick the date of the day first.", which treats date and day as two separate things when the field is labelled "The day" and the heading asks "When is the day?".
findings.fix: Give field() a name argument, field(kids, extra, projectName), with aria-label "The plan for " + (projectName || F.project.name), and pass sibling.name from states["owner-empty"]. Give foot() an optional stamp argument and pass none on owner-empty, so a project with nothing in it reads "Kept by Orla" and "Signal Timeline" and claims no update it never had. Change the refusal string to "Type the date first." Add a gate assertion for owner-empty: the region label, the h1 and the bar all name the same project, and the footer contains no "Updated".

findings.element: the .b-grab word on every owner row, the editor's "What guests see" segment, states.publish and states.ended in render-b.js
findings.problem: One fact, whether a guest can see this, is named four ways across the chain, and one of the names sits on a control that does something else. On the owner row the only visible word is "SHOWN", set as a mono uppercase micro-label identical in treatment to "SAT 1 AUG", while the editor to its left carries a real Shown/Hidden toggle: the same word is a status in one place and a control in another, and pressing the row's "SHOWN" opens the editor rather than toggling anything, which is what its own accessible name admits when it ends "Open to change it." On publish the eyebrow "What lands in the message" is repeated verbatim as the first six words of the body beneath it ("This is what lands in the message."), and the second eyebrow, "The moment it becomes theirs", is the lab's own caption for this state lifted onto the product surface, where it also collides with "moment" as the noun for a row ("Add a moment", "Delete this moment"). On the ended screen three consecutive sentences use three different words for one event: "turned off", "no longer shared here", "not public any more". And "Nothing you saw before has been deleted" presupposes the reader opened the link before, when the likeliest reader of a dead link is someone opening it for the first time.
findings.fix: Settle on the owner's vocabulary, shown to guests and hidden from guests, and use nothing else. On the row, render the word only when the item is hidden ("Hidden from guests"), so a shown item carries no badge that reads as an untouched toggle, and rewrite grabLabel to lead with the verb the control performs: "Open " + title + ". " + long date + ", in " + dayCount + ". " + (hidden ? "Hidden from guests." : "Shown to guests."). On publish, cut "This is what lands in the message. " from .b-pressBody so it opens "It carries the day, the distance and the plan...", and replace the eyebrow "The moment it becomes theirs" with "The link". On ended, rewrite to one word for one fact: "This link has been turned off." / "The plan for Mara & Finn is not shared here any more. Orla can send a new link whenever they want to." / "Nothing has been deleted. Only the link stopped working." Add gate assertions that no state uses both "public" and "shared" for the same fact and that the publish body does not repeat its own heading.

biggestWin: The voice at rest is the real thing, and it does work no other seat's material can do. "Kept by Orla" turns a footer into a person taking responsibility. "Here is everything, love. It updates itself." is a sentence an actual planner would type, and it carries the whole promise in six words. "Bringing in what is ahead." refuses the shimmer-and-lie loading register. "You can turn the link off at any time. Anyone holding it then sees that it has ended." states a consequence most products would bury. Best of all is the split fold in behindBlock: the owner gets a tally ("2 done, the last of them 18 April.") and the guest gets the thing itself ("The Orchard reserved, 18 April."), because a couple who have never used a tracker should never be handed a score. That is judgement, not word choice. The palette is spent rather than merely obeyed: across a whole received phone screen indigo appears exactly twice, as the rule under the horizon and the one filled tick on the next thing, and it never sets a letter, so the accent still means something on the eleventh screen, which is the test nearly every ink-and-white product fails by the third.
